text: A woman disappears, and the detective assigned to the case ends up auditing four marriages instead. Valerie Somers has been carrying the murder of her daughter for a long time, and has begun to suspect her husband John of an affair; when she is gone, Leon Zat picks it up. The two hours go mostly to the couples the search touches, each protecting something small and shabby, and the investigation works less as a puzzle than as a warrant to knock on doors and watch faces do their work. Ray Lawrence declines to score points. Nobody is unmasked as a monster; people are shown lying about the things people lie about, which is harder to film and harder to watch. Three of the acting prizes at the Australian awards went to this cast, lead and supporting both, and that is the honest measure of where the weight sits.

A western in which the man being run down belongs to the country being ridden across. In 1929 an Aboriginal stockman kills a white station owner in self-defence and takes off, with a posse behind him on horseback. The genre's furniture is all present — the chase, the tracker, the long ride — and every piece of it means something else under those terms. It won for cinematography, and the images earn that without prettiness: distance here is information about how far away help is. A hundred and thirteen minutes, most of them in motion. What Warwick Thornton is driving at is narrower than guilt. The question is whether a man in this position will be permitted to have acted in self-defence at all, and who will be doing the deciding on the road back.

The nesting is the design: a narrator, then his ancestors on a goose hunt in Australia's Northern Territory, then inside that a story from further back again. What each layer is for arrives slowly, and none of it is decoration. A young man on the hunt wants his elder brother's wife, and rather than forbid him an elder starts talking, because the correction this culture uses is a tale about what happened the last time. Customary law delivered as narrative instead of sentence. Ninety minutes, at the pace of the hunt itself, and the register is comic far more often than solemn. Direction, editing and camera all took awards, which are precisely the three crafts that had to hold three time frames apart while a viewer moves between them, and Australian critics have since put the film in their twenty-five best of the century.

Heat, a weekend, and four friends who have each just been handed news that rearranges the shape of a life. The scale stays domestic on purpose: no investigation, no sirens, only the hours after the phone call when the ordinary business of a Saturday still has to be got through. Sarah Watt runs it at a hundred minutes, enough for four strands and not enough for any of them to harden into a case study. The weather does structural work. Everything happens inside a temperature nobody can step out of, and the film uses that the way another film would use a deadline. Both lead acting awards went to it, the right address for the credit, since a premise this quiet lives on faces. What is at stake is not survival but composure, on a day when nobody has anything spare.

A respected eye doctor wants out of an affair and discovers that wanting is not sufficient. Running beside him, in a track the film keeps stubbornly separate, a documentary maker courts a television producer while shooting a portrait of her insufferably self-centered boss. The halves match in structure and differ in weight, and the comedy is not relief from the other story; it is evidence about what a person will settle for. Handing the first man an ophthalmologist's practice is a joke made early and then not treated as one. A hundred and four minutes, cut so that a moral crisis and a run of small humiliations keep interrupting each other, neither granted the dignity of its own act. Screenwriters have kept the script on their list of the hundred and one best, and it holds a place on TSPDT's thousand.

December 22nd, sixteen years on, and a provincial television station has decided to settle on air whether the revolution happened in their town or only somewhere else. The guests are a history teacher losing ground to his debts and a pensioner with another Christmas alone in front of him. Neither is anyone's idea of a witness to history, which is the joke, and then stops being one. Corneliu Porumboiu keeps the question small: not what the revolution meant, only whether anyone in this particular square came out before it was safe to. Eighty-nine minutes. The comedy runs on vanity, on corrections, on the pauses of men holding a version of themselves in place while a camera is on. It took the Caméra d'Or, and Romanian critics have since put it among the ten best films the country has made.

A romance whose two Academy honors went to black-and-white photography and to special effects. That means the impossible thing in it was solved with a camera rather than argued in dialogue. The premise fits on a line: a struggling painter, a girl he cannot account for, and the pictures he starts making because of her. Eighty-six minutes, 1948, and the four labels it carries, drama and romance and fantasy and mystery, behave less like a mixture than a sequence, each taking over as the one before stops being adequate. Effects here are not spectacle. At this size they are the machinery by which a face is permitted to stay uncertain, and that uncertainty is the whole transaction. It carries the Volpi Cup for Best Actor and a long-held place on TSPDT's thousand greatest.

Natalie fixes pipes for a living; her twin sister Nicola does not work at all, and one house north of London has to hold both of them. Their mother clerks in a shop. Their father cooks, and keeps not finishing the improvements he began. That is the entire apparatus, and Mike Leigh runs it for a hundred and three minutes without granting anyone the speech that would explain them. The comedy is exact rather than kind: people are funny in the same specifics that make them difficult, and nothing steps in to sort out which is which. The BFI keeps it among the hundred best British films, and the National Society of Film Critics called it the best picture of its year. What it tests is whether ordinary fondness holds up under daily proximity, when one person at the table has stopped moving and everyone can see it.

Colour film, made in Britain in 1944, about an English king taking an army across the Channel and winning. The honors say what kind of object this is: art direction in colour, an original dramatic score, and the lead performance, which Laurence Olivier gave himself while directing. The archaic title it carried, a chronicle history with the battle fought at Agincourt, announces a text written to be spoken, and turning speech into two hours and seventeen minutes of picture means deciding constantly when to trust the language and when to spend money on it. The 1415 campaign supplies the events. The pressure comes from a young king having to convince tired men that a claim on paper is worth their bodies. The National Board of Review named it the best film of its year; the BFI has it among the hundred best British ones.

Two hours and forty-six minutes for a story about whom a woman with land will marry. The length is arithmetic rather than padding: Bathsheba Everdine comes into a large farm without expecting to, and the seasons need room enough that her choices read as decisions taken across years instead of moods taken in an afternoon. Three men, unalike in every respect that counts, each of whom would make her a different kind of owner. The BFI keeps the film among the hundred best British ones, and the score took an Academy honor, which matters at this length, because music is load-bearing here and carries stretches dialogue does not. Underneath the courtships John Schlesinger is filming labour: a holding where one bad night undoes a year, and where a marriage is also a decision about who runs the place.

A film about a painter that wins its prize for cinematography has either made a joke about itself or accepted a dare. This one accepted. It takes the last twenty-five years of J.M.W. Turner and gives them a hundred and fifty minutes without the shape a life usually gets on screen: no ascent, no breakthrough, a man continuing to work while everyone around him gets older. Two households, in effect. A housekeeper whose devotion goes unreturned and unacknowledged, and a landlady at the coast whom he does not announce to anyone. Mike Leigh lets him be graceless without making the gracelessness the thesis. The costumes and the score were honored as well. But the light is the argument: a painter's problem happening to an actual sky, in front of a camera that has to solve it a second time.

Ernesto's job is to take bones out of the ground and give names back to them. It is 2018 in Guatemala, officers are on trial for starting the war, and testimony is arriving at the Forensic Foundation faster than the work can absorb it. Then an old woman tells him something that touches his own case: his father vanished as a guerrilla fighter, and a lead on that is the one thing a man in Ernesto's position is not supposed to be looking for. Seventy-eight minutes, with nothing decorative in them. The pressure is procedural before it is emotional, since the method that makes his findings hold up depends on his not being anybody's son. César Díaz took the Caméra d'Or for it, and it went forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards. A country is trying to hold a trial and a private grief in one room.

A game show called Twenty-One, a champion the producers have chosen in advance, and a country watching it happen. Herbert Stempel holds the title until he is replaced by a more presentable contestant, Charles Van Doren, and being discarded is what converts him into a witness. Richard Goodwin, a lawyer, goes looking for the arrangement behind the broadcast. Robert Redford films a class story wearing a scandal's clothes: what Van Doren has and Stempel does not is not intelligence but the look of belonging, and a network is buying that look by the week. A hundred and thirty-three minutes, talk-driven, patient with rooms. New York critics named it the best film of its year. The interest is not in who cheated, settled early, but in what each man will trade for the appearance of deserving it.

Tereza is brought back to Prague by a man with no intention of giving anything up, and she learns what that means soon after she arrives. Tomas is a surgeon whose arrangement with his own life requires that nothing weigh very much: Sabina, the others, no consequences that stick. Then the tanks come, and lightness stops being a policy anyone can maintain. Philip Kaufman spends a hundred and seventy-one minutes here, and the length is the method. The erotic scenes and the political ones get the same attention and the same duration, so that a decision about a lover and a decision about a country stop being different sizes. The cinematography prize recognized a texture: handled, close, warm and short of air. The National Society of Film Critics named it the best picture of its year.
